title: 1 Chronicles 24:20–31
context: The chapter ends with a list of the rest of the sons of Levi, family heads from the lines of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, Uzziel, and Merari, many of whom appear in slightly different forms in 23:7–23, such as Shubael for Shebuel and Shelomoth for Shelomith, along with a few names not found there, such as Jaaziah. These Levites also cast lots in the presence of David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the priests and Levites, with the chief and the younger brother treated alike. The text does not explain the differences between the two lists or how the lots were used for the Levites. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about equal standing in service and the careful ordering of worship. The emphasis on impartiality suggests that every household, senior or junior, had a recognized place before the LORD.

verses.text: Of the rest of the sons of Levi: of the sons of Amram, Shubael; of the sons of Shubael, Jehdeiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the rest of the sons of Levi listed, beginning with Shubael of Amram’s line. The record extends beyond the priests.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of the Levites as honoring their role alongside the priests. Both traditions commonly note that Shubael corresponds closely to Shebuel in 23:16.

verses.text: Of Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, Isshiah the chief.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isshiah named as chief of the sons of Rehabiah. Leadership continues within each family from one generation to the next.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the naming of chiefs as preserving order in service. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the continuing genealogy.

verses.text: Of the Izharites, Shelomoth; of the sons of Shelomoth, Jahath.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Shelomoth of the Izharites and his son Jahath. Each family line is carefully recorded for its place in service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as reflecting continuity across generations. Both traditions commonly note that Shelomoth corresponds to Shelomith in 23:18.

verses.text: The sons of Hebron: Jeriah, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Hebron listed in order, first through fourth. The same names appear in the earlier list at 23:19.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the consistency between lists as reflecting stable family identities. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the ordered record.

verses.text: The sons of Uzziel: Micah; of the sons of Micah, Shamir.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Micah of Uzziel’s line and his son Shamir. The list continues to trace each family with steady care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the genealogy as preserving those called to serve. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a careful account.

verses.text: The brother of Micah: Isshiah; of the sons of Isshiah, Zechariah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isshiah, Micah’s brother, and his son Zechariah. Brothers and their descendants share together in service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of brothers as showing that God’s calling extends across families. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the complete list.

verses.text: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The son of Jaaziah: Beno.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Merari listed, with Beno the son of Jaaziah. A name not found in the earlier list appears here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the addition of Jaaziah as part of a fuller record of Merari’s line. Both traditions commonly leave the differences between the lists unresolved, as the text does.

verses.text: The sons of Merari by Jaaziah: Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Merari by Jaaziah named. Even lesser-known families are included in the record of service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as showing that no household is overlooked in God’s service. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the expanded genealogy.

verses.text: Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Eleazar of Mahli’s line had no sons. The record honestly notes family limitations without hiding them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the note as consistent with 23:22, where his daughters married within the family. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a truthful record.

verses.text: Of Kish, the son of Kish: Jerahmeel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Jerahmeel named as the son of Kish. The line of Kish continues in service through the next generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the continuation as fulfilling the provision noted in 23:22. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the careful genealogy.

verses.text: The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites after their fathers’ houses.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Mushi listed, concluding the Levite families. The record of Levite service is now complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary as affirming the order of the Levites. Both traditions commonly note that Jerimoth corresponds to Jeremoth in 23:23.

verses.text: These likewise cast lots even as their brothers the sons of Aaron in the presence of David the king, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the fathers’ households of the priests and of the Levites, the fathers’ households of the chief even as those of his younger brother.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites casting lots like their brothers the priests, with the chief and the younger treated alike. Fairness extends to every household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the impartial lot as honoring God’s ordering over human status (compare Proverbs 16:33). Readers in both traditions commonly note that the text does not explain how the lots were used for the Levites.
